content: Ulcerative colitis predominantly affects individuals who do not smoke. Patients who smoke intermittently often report an improvement in their symptoms during periods of smoking. Additionally, nonsmokers with ulcerative colitis who begin smoking may experience remission of their disease. To investigate this phenomenon, randomized controlled trials were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of transdermal nicotine in inducing remission in patients with ulcerative colitis. The primary objective of these studies was to determine whether transdermal nicotine could effectively induce remission in patients with ulcerative colitis. A secondary objective was to assess the adverse events associated with transdermal nicotine therapy in this patient population. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using the MEDLINE (via PubMed) and EMBASE databases with the terms ulcerative colitis and transdermal nicotine or nicotine. The search included publications from 1970 to June 2008. Additional studies were identified through manual searches of reference lists from relevant papers and abstracts from major gastroenterological meetings. The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and the Cochrane Inflammatory Bowel Disease Group Specialized Trials Register were also searched. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials involving patients with active mild to moderate ulcerative colitis. Participants were randomly assigned to receive transdermal nicotine (15 to 25 mg/day), a placebo, or another treatment such as corticosteroids or mesalamine. Data extraction and quality assessment of the trials were performed independently by the authors, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients achieving clinical or sigmoidoscopic remission, as defined by the individual studies. Secondary outcomes included clinical response, adverse events, and withdrawal due to adverse events. Nine studies were identified, of which five met the inclusion criteria. A meta-analysis of two trials, involving 71 patients treated with nicotine and 70 patients treated with placebo, demonstrated a statistically significant benefit of nicotine therapy. After four to six weeks of treatment, 19 out of 71 patients receiving transdermal nicotine achieved clinical remission, compared to 9 out of 70 patients receiving placebo (odds ratio [OR] = 2.56, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02–6.45). Additionally, improvement or remission was observed in 29 out of 71 patients treated with nicotine, compared to 14 out of 70 patients treated with placebo (OR = 2.72, 95% CI 1.28–5.81). Among patients with left-sided colitis, the odds ratio for improvement or remission was 2.31 (95% CI 1.05–5.10). However, when transdermal nicotine was compared to standard medical therapy (oral prednisone or mesalamine), no significant benefit was observed. After four to six weeks of treatment, 34 out of 63 patients receiving standard therapy achieved clinical or sigmoidoscopic remission, compared to 33 out of 66 patients treated with transdermal nicotine (OR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.37–1.60). A meta-analysis of all five studies, which included 137 patients treated with transdermal nicotine and 133 patients treated with placebo or standard therapy, showed no statistically significant benefit of nicotine therapy (OR = 1.23, 95% CI 0.71–2.14). Patients treated with transdermal nicotine were significantly more likely to withdraw from treatment due to adverse events compared to those receiving placebo or standard medical therapy (OR = 5.82, 95% CI 1.66–20.47). Furthermore, patients receiving transdermal nicotine were significantly more likely to experience adverse events than those treated with placebo or standard therapy (OR = 3.54, 95% CI 2.07–6.08). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that transdermal nicotine is more effective than placebo in inducing remission in patients with ulcerative colitis. However, no significant advantage was observed when transdermal nicotine was compared to standard medical therapy. The high incidence of adverse events associated with transdermal nicotine limits its utility in some patients.
